messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] effect size estimation for linked QTL
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] effect size estimation for linked QTL
messages.body_plain:
Without code, it's hard to know exactly what you're doing or the cause of the differences you're seeing.
But in general it's better to derive effect estimates in the multiple-QTL model, and this is for sure true in the case of linked QTL.

The percent variance explained by the individual QTL is difficult to derive in the case of linked QTL, and the values that fitqtl() gives are not trustworthy.
Such heritabilities generally don't add up, but particularly they won't be additive when the QTL are linked.

I don't understand why you say "link QTL in repulsion" because these two QTL look to be in linked coupling (effects in the same direction).

karl

> On Apr 30, 2018, at 10:43 AM, Mingzi Xu <xu4...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I have a question about estimating effect sizes for two linked QTL in repulsion on the same linkage group. In one of the crosses, scantwo and MQM converge on a model with two QTL ~25cM apart on the same linkage group. There are enough recombinant individuals between the two markers that I think both of them are real. There is no interaction between the two QTL. The problem comes when I try to estimate the effect sizes of these two QTL.
>
> When I look at the phenotypic values at 3 genotypes for each closest marker, I got:
> 5...@1.1
>
> $Means
>
> S006407_145458.AA S006407_145458.AB S006407_145458.BB <http://S006407_145458.BB>
>
>          3.297125          3.581586          3.764132
>
> $SEs
>
> S006407_145458.AA S006407_145458.AB S006407_145458.BB <http://S006407_145458.BB>
>
>        0.02396367        0.01700716        0.02686074
>
>
>
> 5...@26.4
>
> $Means
>
> S000353_224758.AA S000353_224758.AB S000353_224758.BB <http://S000353_224758.BB>
>
>          3.166557          3.537672          3.902117
>
> $SEs
>
> S000353_224758.AA S000353_224758.AB S000353_224758.BB <http://S000353_224758.BB>
>
>
>       0.011397453       0.007839206       0.010864514
>
>
> In the MQM model with no interaction, I got the following estimations from fitqtl function:
> Estimated effects:
>
> -----------------
>
>                 est        SE       t
>
> Intercept  3.538364  0.005403 654.828
>
> 5...@1.1a     0.044956  0.009370   4.798
>
> 5...@1.1d     0.030052  0.011184   2.687
>
> 5...@26.4a    0.341736  0.009104  37.536
>
> 5...@26.4d   -0.008532  0.011086  -0.770
>
> And the two QTL together explain 88% of the F2 variance.
>
> However, the additive effect size for the first QTL is much smaller than what the marker phenotype suggests. I thought this may has something to do with two linked QTL violating the assumption of independence. So I estimated the effect size of each QTL from a model that just includes one QTL at a time (using the same fitqtl function). This seems to give me more reasonable effect size estimation:
> Estimated effects:
>
> -----------------
>
>               est      SE       t
>
> Intercept 3.55611 0.01243 286.010
>
> 5...@1.1a    0.23350 0.01808  12.915
>
> 5...@1.1d    0.05096 0.02488   2.048
>
>
> Estimated effects:
>
> -----------------
>
>                est       SE       t
>
> Intercept 3.536018 0.005583 633.325
>
> 5...@26.4a   0.367744 0.007912  46.477
>
> 5...@26.4d   0.003318 0.011163   0.297
>
>
>
> However, the sum of additive effects of the two QTL is > parental difference and the % of F2 variance explained by each QTL is >100% (31% for 5...@1.1 and 87% for 5...@26.4) in models with just one QTL, which is hard to interpret when the model suggests two QTL with no interaction.
>
>
>
> I wonder what is the source of the discrepancy in effect size from MQM model estimation and from phenotype of the closest marker, and what effect size is most sound to report, from marker phenotype, fitqtl with both QTL or fitqtl with each locus?
>
>
>
> Many thanks!
>
>

This suggests two QTL with no interaction.

I then did MQM starting with the significant QTL from scanone:

> qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.sim.02<-sim.geno(qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.gp.02,step=0.2,n.draw=10000,map.function=c("kosambi"),err=0.001)

> qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.refine1.02<-refineqtl(qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.sim.02,qtl=qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.make1.02,formula=y~Q1,verbose=FALSE)

> qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.add1<-addqtl(qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.sim.02,qtl=qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.refine1.02,formula=y~Q1+Q2)

then add a second QTL indicated from the addqtl function

> qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.make2.02<-makeqtl(qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.sim.02,chr=c(5,5),pos=c(1.09,26.4))

> qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.refine2.02<-refineqtl(qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.sim.02,qtl=qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.make2.02,formula=y~Q1+Q2,verbose=FALSE)

Then, addint function indicates no interaction between the two QTL and addqtl function indicates no additional QTL. This model corroborates with what scantwo indicates.

The effect sizes of the two QTL are estimated with the following code:

> qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.fit2.eff<-fitqtl(qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.sim.02,qtl=qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.refine2.02,formula=y~Q1+Q2,dropone=FALSE,get.est=TRUE)

5...@1.1a     0.044956  0.009370   4.798

5...@26.4a    0.341736  0.009104  37.536

5...@26.4d   -0.008532  0.011086  -0.770

The additive effect of the QTL at 5...@26.4 is similar to the phenotypes of the closet marker

> qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.q2.eff<-effectplot(qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.sim.02,mname1="S000353_224758",draw=FALSE)

> qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.q2.eff

$Means

S000353_224758.AA S000353_224758.AB S000353_224758.BB <http://S000353_224758.BB>

         3.166557          3.537672          3.902117

$SEs

S000353_224758.AA S000353_224758.AB S000353_224758.BB <http://S000353_224758.BB>

      0.011397453       0.007839206       0.010864514

But such is not the case for QTL at 5...@1.1. The phenotype of its closest marker (at 1.09 cM) indicates much larger effect size (~0.23) then the fitqtl function suggests (0.05)

> qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.q1.eff<-effectplot(qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.sim.02,mname1="S006407_145458",draw=FALSE)

> qtl4c.9.m.chr5.o.q1.eff

$Means

S006407_145458.AA S006407_145458.AB S006407_145458.BB <http://S006407_145458.BB>

         3.297125          3.581586          3.764132
$SEs

S006407_145458.AA S006407_145458.AB S006407_145458.BB <http://S006407_145458.BB>

       0.02396367        0.01700716        0.02686074

I'm trying to understand why the fitqtl function using the final MQM gives such different estimation from what the marker phenotype suggests for the QTL at 1.1 cM, especially there is no interaction between the two QTL. Is there a mistake in the code? And I'm sorry that I meant to say that the two QTL are linked in coupling, not repulsion.

messages.subject: Re: Genetic map in Maize with a high density of SNPs and RILs
messages.subject_clean: Genetic map in Maize with a high density of SNPs and RILs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

Ive just wanted to ask you one more thing.

I have the physical location and the chromosome of each marker. So, I have been working chromosome by chromosome so as to avoid long hours of computing time.

I have previously delete markers with missing data, monomorphic markers for both parents, and those markers with wrong segregation. Also the duplicated markers!...

When constructing my genetic map, frstly, I tried using ripple function to asign a specific order and then calculate the cM for a qtl analysis. But the lenght of my genetic map was really high.

Then, I order my markers based on their physical position and then calculated the cM. And the lenght of my map was much better.

So, I constructed my map using the order I asigned based on their physical position instead of using ripple function.

Is this correct?

Thanks for everything
Lucas A.

On Wednesday, January 17, 2018 at 10:07:31 PM UTC-3, Lucas A. wrote:
> Hi Karl,
>
> I am trying to make a genetic map in Maize with 164 RILs and a high density of SNPs.
>
> I started out with 56.000 markers. I eliminated almost 40.000 markers due to missing data, monomorphic markers for both parents, and those markers with wrong segregation.
>
> I finally got 12.455 SNPs (distributed in the 10 maize chromosomes). I have got the chromosomes location for each marker, and also the physic distance of each marker.
>
> I would like to calculate the genetic distance of each marker, so as to later do a QTL analysis.
>
> I have been able to correctly use the function read.cross() and jittermap() functions. But I am having a bit of trouble using the est.rf, and others functions. My computer is not too good and I am working with a lot of markers (12.455 SNPs for the genetic map).
>
> This is the error I’ve got when running est.rf() function: Error: cannot allocate vector of size 926.7 Mb.
>
> I was just wondering if I can continue my analysis working with each chromosome separately.
>
> Or maybe there is a way of reducing those 12.455 markers to a fewer number, so I can continue working with less markers. I dont know if there is a function to do this or if it is reazonable to do it.
>
> What do you recommend me?
>
> Thanks a lot,
> Lucas A.

messages.subject: covariates and the X chromosome
messages.body_plain:
I have a dataset that consists of only males and only X-linked markers (so haploid genotypes).  I have successfully used scanone with either a normal or 2part model, but am encountering challenges when I try to add a covariate to the analysis.  This produces a warning ("X'X matrix is singular"), and the resulting output consists of a lod score of 943.9 for every position on the genetic map.

Is there an obvious solution?  I am using R/qtl ... would this approach work better with R/qtl2?

thanks so much,

Colin

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] covariates and the X chromosome
messages.body_plain:
As currently implemented, scanone with the 2-part model can't take covariates.

You could try the approximation: define the two derived traits (the binary trait of 0 vs >0, and the quantitative trait for values >0), and use scanone with them, with the covariate.

karl

messages.subject: penalty LOD for MQM including a covariate
messages.subject_clean: penalty LOD for MQM including a covariate
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl and R/qtl community,

I have a question about how to calculate penalty LOD for mqm model including a covariate. As scantwo (with addcovar=sex) reveals a significant pair of interacting QTLs, I included them in the MQM model, which also included sex as a covariate.  And from the drop-one analysis, I got the following result.

> fitqtl(t2.sim, qtl=rqtl,formula=y~Q1:Q2+sex,pheno.col = 17,covar = sex)
########################################################################
		fitqtl summary

Method: multiple imputation
Model:  normal phenotype
Number of observations : 170

Full model result
----------------------------------
Model formula: y ~ Q1 + Q2 + sex + Q1:Q2

       df       SS         MS      LOD     %var Pvalue(Chi2)    Pvalue(F)
Model  16 10.67527 0.66720461 22.49767 45.63473 7.327472e-15 1.130207e-13
Error 153 12.71760 0.08312157
Total 169 23.39287

Drop one QTL at a time ANOVA table:
----------------------------------
              df Type III SS   LOD  %var F value Pvalue(Chi2) Pvalue(F)
5...@60.6        12       5.397 13.06 23.07   5.411            0  1.29e-07 ***
9...@17.4        12       5.396 13.06 23.07   5.410            0  1.29e-07 ***
sex  1       5.474 13.21 23.40  65.854            0  1.48e-13 ***
5...@60.6:9...@17.4  9       4.561 11.31 19.50   6.097            0  2.63e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

########################################################################

I also got the penalty score from 1000 permutations in scantwo (with addcovar=sex). So If I want to calculate the pLOD score for the current MQM model, it should be like pLOD = LOD for MQM - (main*2 + light). But regarding LOD for MQM, should I use the overall LOD score (22.49) or overall LOD - (LOD for sex), which is 22.49-13.21 in this case?

Thank you very much for your attention.

Best,
Ivan

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] penalty LOD for MQM including a covariate
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] penalty LOD for MQM including a covariate
messages.body_plain:
I would recommend keeping sex as a covariate in all models, and using that overall LOD score (22.49767 in this case) in your calculation of the penalized LOD. What matters are differences in the penalized LOD scores, rather than absolutes.

22.49-13.21 is the LOD score for the model with the chr 5 and 9 QTL and their interaction, but without sex. When you look at a different model, say with just the chr 5 QTL, you'll find that the LOD score for sex in the drop-one-qtl table will be a bit different, and you want to compare the different models with sex included.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

Thanks for your answer. When comparing different models based on penalized LOD, it is ok to use overall LOD score include sex in all models.

But how about comparing with null model? I guess the null model should include sex then. The penalized LOD score will be:

 overall LOD (chr 5 and 9 QTL and their interaction plus sex) - LOD (sex alone) - (2*main+light)

Does it make sense? It seems that is the way how stepwiseqtl calculates.

Thank you again.

Best,
Ivan

On Saturday, May 12, 2018 at 8:01:36 PM UTC+2, Karl Broman wrote:

> I would recommend keeping sex as a covariate in all models, and using that overall LOD score (22.49767 in this case) in your calculation of the penalized LOD. What matters are differences in the penalized LOD scores, rather than absolutes.
>
> 22.49-13.21 is the LOD score for the model with the chr 5 and 9 QTL and their interaction, but without sex. When you look at a different model, say with just the chr 5 QTL, you'll find that the LOD score for sex in the drop-one-qtl table will be a bit different, and you want to compare the different models with sex included.
